title: De-extinction: the plan to bring back mammoth-like elephants and the debate around it

sources.title: Hoping to revive woolly mammoths, scientists start with 'woolly mice' (2025-03-04)
'Woolly mice' were just a start. De-extinction still faces many hurdles (2025)
Genetically engineered woolly mouse is a step toward resurrecting extinct mammoth, company says (2025-03-04)

facts.text: The last woolly mammoths died out roughly 4,000 years ago.
The Asian elephant is the woolly mammoth's closest living relative.
Mammoth remains frozen in permafrost have lost every living cell over thousands of years, so a mammoth cannot be cloned.
A company, Colossal Biosciences, compares mammoth DNA with elephant DNA to find genes behind traits such as long woolly hair and body fat that helped mammoths survive the cold.
The plan is to edit Asian elephant embryos and implant them in female elephants so they give birth to calves with mammoth traits.
In March 2025 the company announced mice with long, woolly, golden hair, three times as long as that of ordinary lab mice.
Mammoths may have been keystone species that shaped the mammoth steppe, the rich northern grassland they lived on.
Supporters argue that herds of mammoth-like animals would press down the snow and grass that insulate frozen ground, so the ground would melt more slowly and release less carbon.
Supporters say the same technologies could help protect species that are alive today.
Critics say editing some genes in an elephant can only make a rough copy of a mammoth, because many genes act together and it is still unknown which genes set mammoths apart.
A critic pointed out that the woolly mouse study did not test whether the mice could tolerate cold.
An Asian elephant pregnancy can last about 22 months, and Asian elephants are listed as endangered.
Elephants have social knowledge passed down through generations, and an ecologist said an edited elephant could not be taught to be a mammoth.
The Pleistocene epoch, the time of the last ice age, ended about 11,700 years ago, and the northern landscape has changed greatly since then.
Some critics say the money would do more good if used to protect species that are disappearing now; one called de-extinction a distraction from conservation.
An ice age ecologist said she would be excited to see a mammoth in person, yet doubts that the planned animals would count as true mammoths.
